title: Best Breast Pumps UK
short: Six wearable and electric breast pumps tested by breastfeeding mums over weeks and months, compared on comfort, discretion, output and price.
intro: Whether you're exclusively pumping, expressing at work or just want the flexibility of an occasional bottle, the right pump makes a big difference. This guide is based on Mumsnet's tested roundup (updated July 2026), where breastfeeding mums used wearable, electric and manual pumps in daily real-life use over several weeks to months, judging comfort, discretion, durability, ease of washing and value for money. Mumsnet also drew on advice from lactation consultant and midwife Milly Godwin. You don't need a pump if breastfeeding is going well, and if you have concerns about feeding or supply, speak to a lactation consultant, midwife or health visitor. Prices are those quoted at time of writing.

products.name: Motion InBra Breast Pump
products.best_for: Regular pumpers who want a quiet, discreet, fully hands-free pump
products.key_spec: Wearable, rechargeable, single or double, 0 to 300 mmHg, two stimulation and nine suction levels, closed system
products.summary: Mumsnet's top tested wearable. A mum of two used it over eight months and gave it almost perfect scores, calling it 'as discreet as a breast pump could be'. Thoughtful touches include lights to guide placement in the dark and a vibration warning if you tip too far forward and risk leaks. The parent-tester rated it 10/10. The price is steep for occasional use and the battery can run down quickly if left unused.
pros: Compact and easy to wear under a bra
Easy to clean with fully submersible parts
cons: Some thin plastic parts need careful handling
May feel expensive for occasional use

products.name: Wearable Electric Breast Pump
products.best_for: Newborn feeding and anyone wanting hands-free pumping at a lower price
products.key_spec: Wearable, rechargeable, single or double, 0 to 280 mmHg, four stimulation and nine suction levels, LED display
products.summary: Mumsnet's parent-tester used it extensively from the first days of her son's life and found it easy to use, comfortable and efficient, saying it made a difference to feeding her newborn and made it easy for her husband to feed him too. It's a relatively inexpensive alternative to Elvie, Momcozy and Medela, with 25 storage bags and a 160ml bottle included. It only comes with one flange size.
pros: Extremely easy to set up and use
cons: Only comes with one choice of flange size

products.name: S2 Pro Wearable Breast Pump
products.best_for: Regular pumpers who want warming, massage, strong output and long battery life
products.key_spec: Double wearable, four modes, 10 suction levels up to 300 mmHg, HeatFlow 2.0 warming, wireless charging case
products.summary: Mumsnet's tester used it while exclusively breastfeeding her five-month-old and building a freezer stash. Over several weeks she regularly expressed about 5oz (150ml) in five minutes and called it the best pump she'd used, even better than manual ones in her opinion. Battery life was outstanding and the fit was secure and leak-free. It's expensive, the maximum suction may feel too intense for some, and it's still visible under clothing.
pros: Excellent milk output and fast pumping times
Useful wireless charging case and outstanding battery life
cons: Expensive compared to many breast pumps
Maximum suction may feel too intense for some users

products.name: Air 1 Ultra-Slim Breast Pump
products.best_for: Anyone who puts discretion first and wants a slim pump under everyday clothing
products.key_spec: Ultra-slim wearable, up to 285 mmHg, three modes and nine suction levels, 200ml per pump, charging case, app
products.summary: Mumsnet's tester used it for six weeks while exclusively breastfeeding her three-month-old and caring for a two-year-old, and found it 'definitely one of the slimmest ones' on the market. It expressed a full feed in around 20 minutes and gave enough battery for roughly five sessions between charges. The app adds reminders and routines. The main drawback is the price, considerably more than models like the Momcozy S12 Pro.

pros: Ultra-slim design that is quiet, discreet and comfortable to wear
cons: Can be messy to pour milk out

products.name: 2-in-1 Double Electric Breast Pump
products.best_for: Anyone who wants a traditional hospital-grade style double electric pump for under £150
products.key_spec: Double electric, battery or mains, 55 to 220 mmHg, three pumping styles, eight suction levels
products.summary: Mumsnet found a smaller, cheaper and easier-to-handle alternative to hospital-grade pumps like the Spectra and Ardo, with a double pump that expresses faster than a single and milk going straight into a Lansinoh bottle. It's easy to assemble with three pumping styles. It isn't hands-free, and some reviewers had to lean forward or hold the bottles, resulting in back pain.
pros: Not too pricey compared with other hospital-grade pumps
cons: Can be tricky to use hands-free, particularly as a double pump
Some reviewers had to hold the bottles, resulting in back pain

products.name: M5 Wearable Double Electric Breast Pump
products.best_for: Expressing on the go, at your desk or in public
products.key_spec: Wearable, single or double, up to 270 mmHg, three modes and nine suction levels, 12-month unit warranty
products.summary: Mumsnet's parent-tester, who used a hospital-grade pump every day for six months, found the M5 gets equivalent milk volumes. Testers found it quiet and discreet, small enough to wear out and about, and efficient. The only downside Mumsnet lists is the price.
pros: Small enough to wear out and about

guide.q: Do I need a breast pump?
guide.a: Not necessarily. Lactation consultant Milly Godwin says if your baby is feeding effectively and you have a good supply you may not need to pump. Many mums do use one, for example so a partner can give an evening bottle, or, if a baby isn't feeding effectively, to help stimulate supply.

Wearable pumps like the Medela Motion InBra and Eufy S2 Pro are hands-free and discreet but cost more. A double electric like the Lansinoh 2-in-1 expresses quickly but isn't hands-free. Manual pumps are the cheapest and simplest for occasional use, and Mumsnet's guide also covers the Medela Harmony manual pump.

guide.q: Are wearable pumps as effective as traditional ones?
guide.a: Mumsnet's testers found the best wearables performed well: one mum who had used a hospital-grade pump daily for six months said the Momcozy M5 got equivalent milk volumes, and another found the Eufy S2 Pro better than manual pumps. Results vary by person, so check what a returns policy allows.

guide.q: What should I check before buying?
guide.a: Look at comfort and flange (shield) size, since some pumps like the Lansinoh wearable have only one, and Medela shield sizes cost extra. Also check battery life, noise, how easy the parts are to wash and how visible it is under clothing. If pumping hurts or supply worries you, seek advice from a lactation consultant.
